findings.title: Duplicate-provider error removed, and equal-order providers are now picked arbitrarily
findings.body: The old code threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and takes the first. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two of them are on the classpath, for example FIPS and default through a packaging mistake, the winner depends on the sort being stable over ServiceLoader order, which is classpath order. A FIPS deployment could silently run the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, where it used to fail fast. The ignored providers are reported only at debug level. All providers are also instantiated before the choice (the stream is collected eagerly), and the Default and FIPS constructors register global java.security providers as a side effect. Give the real providers distinct orders, or keep failing when the top order is tied, and log ignored providers at a visible level.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI, and `int order()` is added as an abstract method. Any third-party or downstream implementation (custom FIPS/HSM providers and the like) no longer compiles. A binary that was compiled earlier throws AbstractMethodError inside CryptoIntegration.detectProvider when `CryptoProvider::order` is invoked, which fails startup. A `default int order()` returning a neutral value would keep compatibility while still letting the three built-in providers override it.

findings.title: Most CryptoProvider operations throw UnsupportedOperationException, including plain-JCA ones
findings.body: AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init, so this class becomes the active provider whenever no higher-order provider is on the classpath. getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, createECParams, getPemUtils and getCertificateUtils all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Most of these have trivial plain-JCA implementations, which WildFlyElytronProvider already shows (Signature.getInstance, KeyFactory.getInstance and so on). keycloak-core code that goes through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() for signing, key parsing, EC parameters or PEM/cert handling will fail at runtime with a bare 'Not supported yet.'. Implement the JCA-based methods, or make the failures descriptive and document the supported subset.

findings.title: Dead code: encoded INTEGERs are computed and discarded
findings.body: `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders and throw the results away, since the same values are encoded again in the following writeDerSeq call. They look like leftover debugging and should be removed.

findings.title: Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a self-consistent round trip
findings.body: `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the default curve (P-256), and that same key signs for ES256, ES384 and ES512. For ES384/ES512 the real r/s values are about 32 bytes while the test asks for 48 and 66 byte components, so the padding path is exercised but the truncation and matching-curve paths are not. P-521 signatures also produce a DER sequence longer than 127 bytes, which uses the long-form length code in ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder, and that path is never run. The assertion is only DER->RS->DER->RS, so a symmetric bug in the encoder and decoder would still pass. The test should use secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1 for the corresponding algorithms. It should also compare against known vectors, or against another implementation, and cover small r/s values and values with the high bit set.
